title: "Estimating Integrals"

execute:
  echo: false

toc: true
---

How would you compute
$$
\int_{[0,1]^{20}} e^{-\|x\|^2}\,dx,
$$
an integral over a cube in twenty dimensions? The simplest method is to lay down a grid and add up the values of the integrand on it. But a grid with only ten points along each axis has $10^{20}$ points, and even at a billion function evaluations a second the sum would take three thousand years! By contrast, just thirty thousand random points give the answer to about 1% accuracy. This is the [Monte Carlo principle](../estimating-pi/) at work again.

In this chapter we will see why grids break down as the dimension grows, and how random points get around the problem. We build two estimators out of random points and ask how accurate each one is, which turns out to be a question about variance. We end with quasi-random points, which try to combine the evenness of a grid with the flexibility of random points.



```{ojs}

//| output: false
// The analysis figures (error against work, on log-log axes) are static
// Observable Plot charts with a key under them. These functions read
// chartColors, so every figure built with them redraws on a dark-mode toggle.

// A chart with a key under it (VM.ui.staticKey) and an optional title above.
// The title is a plain div rather than Plot's own `title` option, which
// renders an <h2> and so takes the page's section-heading style.
function intFigure(chart, key, title) {
  const figure = document.createElement("div")
  figure.className = "int-figure"
  if (title) {
    const heading = document.createElement("div")
    heading.className = "int-figure-title"
    heading.textContent = title
    figure.append(heading)
  }
  figure.append(chart, VM.ui.staticKey(key))
  return figure
}

// "10⁻³" for 0.001: tick labels for a log axis whose ticks are powers of ten.
function intPowerOfTen(value) {
  const superscripts = {"-": "⁻", "0": "⁰", "1": "¹", "2": "²", "3": "³", "4": "⁴", "5": "⁵", "6": "⁶", "7": "⁷", "8": "⁸", "9": "⁹"}
  let exponent = ""
  for (const ch of String(Math.round(Math.log10(value)))) exponent += superscripts[ch]
  return `10${exponent}`
}

// Every power of ten from `lo` to `hi`.
function intDecades(lo, hi) {
  const ticks = []
  for (let k = Math.ceil(Math.log10(lo) - 1e-9); k <= Math.floor(Math.log10(hi) + 1e-9); k++) ticks.push(10 ** k)
  return ticks
}

// A log axis over [lo, hi] with a tick at each power of ten inside it.
function intLogAxis(lo, hi, options) {
  return {type: "log", domain: [lo, hi], ticks: intDecades(lo, hi), tickFormat: intPowerOfTen, ...options}
}

// Error against work for several methods. Each of `series` is
// {label, token, points, kind}, with points [{n, error, ...}] and kind:
//   "band"    a random method: its RMS error as a line with dots, over the
//             band between points' lo and hi (the middle 80% of runs);
//   "scatter" a deterministic method, whose error swings from one n to the
//             next: unjoined dots, and the least-squares line through them,
//             solid over the fitted range n ≥ 100 and dashed before it;
//   "line"    a formula: a dashed line.
// `references` are slopes to compare with, {label, order, at}: a muted line
// of slope -order starting at height `at` on the left edge, labelled at its
// right end. The axes are xDomain and yDomain; anything outside is clipped.
function intRateFigure({series, references = [], xDomain, yDomain, xLabel, yLabel, title, height = 300, chartWidth = width}) {
  const marks = []
  const key = []
  for (const s of series) {
    const color = chartColors[s.token]
    // A deterministic error can be exactly zero, which a log axis can't show.
    const rows = []
    for (const p of s.points) {
      if (p.error > 0 && p.n >= xDomain[0] && p.n <= xDomain[1]) rows.push(p)
    }
    if (s.kind === "band") {
      const band = []
      for (const p of rows) band.push({n: p.n, lo: Math.max(p.lo, yDomain[0]), hi: p.hi})
      const bandColor = VM.plotting.alpha(color, 0.15)
      marks.push(Plot.areaY(band, {x: "n", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", fill: bandColor, clip: true}))
      marks.push(Plot.line(rows, {x: "n", y: "error", stroke: color, strokeWidth: 2, clip: true}))
      marks.push(Plot.dot(rows, {x: "n", y: "error", fill: color, r: 2, clip: true}))
      key.push({label: s.label, marks: [
        {mark: "area", fill: bandColor},
        {mark: "line", stroke: color, strokeWidth: 2},
        {mark: "dot", fill: color, r: 2}
      ]})
    } else if (s.kind === "scatter") {
      marks.push(Plot.dot(rows, {x: "n", y: "error", fill: color, r: 2, clip: true}))
      const fit = convergenceFit(s.points)
      if (fit && rows.length > 0) {
        const fitLine = n => 10 ** fit.intercept * n ** -fit.order
        const first = rows[0].n
        const last = rows[rows.length - 1].n
        const from = Math.max(100, first)
        marks.push(Plot.line([{n: from, error: fitLine(from)}, {n: last, error: fitLine(last)}], {x: "n", y: "error", stroke: color, strokeWidth: 2, clip: true}))
        if (first < 100) {
          marks.push(Plot.line([{n: first, error: fitLine(first)}, {n: 100, error: fitLine(100)}], {x: "n", y: "error", stroke: color, strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "6,4", clip: true}))
        }
      }
      key.push({label: s.label, marks: [
        {mark: "line", stroke: color, strokeWidth: 2},
        {mark: "dot", fill: color, r: 2}
      ]})
    } else {
      marks.push(Plot.line(rows, {x: "n", y: "error", stroke: color, strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "6,4", clip: true}))
      key.push({label: s.label, stroke: color, strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "6,4"})
    }
  }
  for (const ref of references) {
    const ends = [
      {n: xDomain[0], error: ref.at},
      {n: xDomain[1], error: ref.at * (xDomain[1] / xDomain[0]) ** -ref.order}
    ]
    marks.push(Plot.line(ends, {x: "n", y: "error", stroke: chartColors.muted, strokeWidth: 1, strokeDasharray: "2,3", clip: true}))
    marks.push(Plot.text([ends[1]], {x: "n", y: "error", text: () => ref.label, textAnchor: "start", dx: 4, fill: chartColors.muted}))
  }
  const chart = Plot.plot(VM.plotting.plotOptions({
    width: chartWidth, height, marginLeft: 50, marginRight: 44, marginBottom: 40,
    x: intLogAxis(xDomain[0], xDomain[1], {label: xLabel, labelAnchor: "center"}),
    y: intLogAxis(yDomain[0], yDomain[1], {label: yLabel}),
    marks
  }))
  return intFigure(chart, key, title)
}

// One readout per series: the fitted order of convergence, minus the slope of
// the least-squares line through its log-log points with n ≥ 100.
function intOrderStats(series) {
  const stats = []
  for (const s of series) {
    const fit = convergenceFit(s.points)
    let value = "—"
    if (fit) value = `order ≈ ${fit.order.toFixed(2)}`
    stats.push({label: s.label, value, title: "minus the slope of the least-squares line through the log-log points with N ≥ 100"})
  }
  return stats
}

// A slider's value once it has paused for 300 ms: for a figure that
// re-simulates on every change, too much for every tick of a drag.
function intPaused(input) {
  return Generators.observe(notify => {
    let timer = null
    const onInput = () => {
      clearTimeout(timer)
      timer = setTimeout(() => notify(input.value), 300)
    }
    notify(input.value)
    input.addEventListener("input", onInput)
    return () => {
      clearTimeout(timer)
      input.removeEventListener("input", onInput)
    }
  })
}

// Sample sizes for the figures: log-spaced, so they read evenly on a log axis.
intCounts = checkpoints(10000)
intCountsLong = checkpoints(100000)
```


## Grids and the curse of dimensionality {#sec-int-grid}

Let us start in one dimension, where we want to compute
$$
I = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx.
$$
Perhaps the simplest numerical method for this is the *midpoint rule*. We cut $[a, b]$ into $N$ cells of width $h = (b-a)/N$, and on each cell we replace $f$ by its value at the center $c_j = a + (j - \tfrac12)h$ of the cell. Adding up the areas of the resulting rectangles gives
$$
M_N = \frac{b-a}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N f(c_j).
$$
@fig-int-riemann shows these rectangles for $\sin x$ on $[0, \pi]$.

```{ojs}
//| output: false
intRiemannCells = 6
```

```{ojs}
{
  const a = 0
  const b = Math.PI
  const h = (b - a) / intRiemannCells

  const curve = []
  for (let k = 0; k <= 300; k++) {
    const x = a + (b - a) * k / 300
    curve.push({x, y: Math.sin(x)})
  }

  // One rectangle per cell, and a dot where it meets the curve, at the
  // cell's center.
  const cells = []
  for (let j = 0; j < intRiemannCells; j++) {
    const left = a + j * h
    const center = left + h / 2
    cells.push({left, right: left + h, center, height: Math.sin(center)})

  const fill = VM.plotting.alpha(chartColors.fn, 0.15)
  const chart = Plot.plot(VM.plotting.plotOptions({

    y: {domain: [0, 1.05], label: null},
    marks: [

      Plot.line(curve, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: chartColors.ink, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.dot(cells, {x: "center", y: "height", fill: chartColors.fn, r: 3.5})
    ]
  }))
  return intFigure(chart, [

    {label: "Midpoint rectangles", marks: [
      {mark: "area", fill},
      {mark: "line", stroke: chartColors.fn, strokeWidth: 1.5},
      {mark: "dot", fill: chartColors.fn, r: 3.5}
    ]}

}
```

How quickly does $M_N$ approach $I$ as we add more points?

::: {#exr-int-midpoint}
## The midpoint rule
Let $I = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$. Cut $[a, b]$ into $N$ cells of width $h = (b-a)/N$ with centers $c_1, \ldots, c_N$, and let $M_N = h\sum_{j=1}^N f(c_j)$ be the midpoint rule. Assume $f$ has as many continuous derivatives as you need.

a. Expand $f(c + t)$ to second order about the center $c$ of one cell and integrate over $-h/2 \le t \le h/2$ to show
$$
\int_{c-h/2}^{c+h/2} f(x)\,dx = h\,f(c) + \frac{h^3}{24}\,f''(c) + O(h^5).
$$
Why does the first-order term contribute nothing? Why is the remainder $O(h^5)$ rather than $O(h^4)$?
b. Sum over the cells to conclude
$$
I - M_N = \frac{h^2}{24}\,\big(f'(b) - f'(a)\big) + O(h^4).
$$
c. Using (b), write the error of the midpoint rule as a power of $N$. By what factor does it shrink when $N$ doubles? How many times more points does one more correct decimal place cost? Compare with the [standard-error exercise](../estimating-pi/#exr-pi-variance) of the last chapter.
:::

::::: {#fig-int-tangent}

```{ojs}
{
  const a = 0
  const b = Math.PI
  const h = (b - a) / intRiemannCells
  const chosen = 1

  const curve = []
  for (let k = 0; k <= 300; k++) {
    const x = a + (b - a) * k / 300
    curve.push({x, y: Math.sin(x)})
  }

  // The same rectangles as @fig-int-riemann. One cell also gets the tangent
  // line at its center, and the trapezoid under that line.
  const cells = []
  for (let j = 0; j < intRiemannCells; j++) {
    const left = a + j * h
    const center = left + h / 2
    cells.push({left, right: left + h, center, height: Math.sin(center)})
  }
  const cell = cells[chosen]
  const tangent = []
  for (const x of [cell.left, cell.right]) {
    tangent.push({x, y: cell.height + Math.cos(cell.center) * (x - cell.center)})
  }

  // The slanted line: the warn color pulled toward the ink color, so it stands out from its fill.
  const tangentStroke = `color-mix(in srgb, ${chartColors.warn} 60%, ${chartColors.ink})`
  const trapezoidFill = VM.plotting.alpha(chartColors.warn, 0.35)
  const chart = Plot.plot(VM.plotting.plotOptions({
    width, height: 300, marginLeft: 40, marginBottom: 40,
    x: {domain: [a, b], label: "x", labelAnchor: "center"},
    y: {domain: [0, 1.05], label: null},
    marks: [
      Plot.areaY(tangent, {x: "x", y1: 0, y2: "y", fill: trapezoidFill}),
      Plot.rect([cell], {x1: "left", x2: "right", y1: 0, y2: "height", fill: "none", stroke: chartColors.fn, strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "6,4"}),
      Plot.line(tangent, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: tangentStroke, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.line(curve, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: chartColors.ink, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.dot([cell], {x: "center", y: "height", fill: chartColors.fn, r: 3.5})
    ]
  }))
  return intFigure(chart, [
    {label: "sin x", stroke: chartColors.ink, strokeWidth: 2.5},
    {label: "Midpoint rectangle", stroke: chartColors.fn, strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "6,4"},
    {label: "Tangent at the center and the trapezoid under it", marks: [
      {mark: "area", fill: trapezoidFill},
      {mark: "line", stroke: tangentStroke, strokeWidth: 2.5}
    ]}
  ])
}
```

One cell of the midpoint rule for $\sin x$, with the tangent line at its center.

:::::

::: {#exr-int-concave}
## Over or under?
Let $f$ be concave on $[a, b]$, that is, $f'' \le 0$, as $\sin x$ is on $[0, \pi]$. As in @exr-int-midpoint, $M_N$ is the midpoint rule with $N$ cells for $I = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.

a. From @fig-int-riemann, guess whether $M_N$ overestimates or underestimates $I$ for $\sin x$.
b. The graph of a concave function lies below each of its tangent lines. @fig-int-tangent shows the tangent at the center of one cell. Compare the area of the trapezoid under the tangent with the area of the midpoint rectangle. What do you conclude about $M_N$?
c. Now prove this algebraically, using the expansion in @exr-int-midpoint (a).
d. What happens if $f$ is convex, $f'' \ge 0$?
:::

::: {#exr-int-sine}
## The midpoint rule for $\sin x$
a. For $\sin x$ on $[0, \pi]$, evaluate the leading term $\frac{h^2}{24}\big(f'(b) - f'(a)\big)$ of @exr-int-midpoint (b) at $N = 100$, where $h = (b-a)/N$ is the cell width. Does its sign agree with your answer to @exr-int-concave?
b. How many points does the midpoint rule need for the error in (a) to fall to $0.001$?
:::

You should find that the error of the midpoint rule falls like $N^{-2}$, so one more correct decimal place costs only about 3.2 times as many points. By comparison, the circle estimator of the last chapter requires 100 times as many computations for each extra decimal place. You can watch the rule at work on [Visual Math Lab](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/numerical-integration/index.html?f=sin(x)&a=0&b=pi&max=40&n=12&show=f,midpoint){target="_blank"}. So in one dimension, Riemann sums (and their optimizations) are fast enough for computing integrals.

### The curse of dimensionality {#sec-int-curse}

The trouble starts when we move to higher dimensions. Let $f$ now be a function on the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$, and suppose we want
$$
I = \int_{[0,1]^d} f(x)\,dx.
$$
The midpoint rule generalizes directly. We cut each of the $d$ axes into $m$ cells of width $h = 1/m$, which cuts the cube into $N = m^d$ small cubes, and we replace $f$ on each small cube by its value at the center. Since the cube has volume 1, the estimate $M_N$ is simply the average of $f$ over the $N$ centers.

How accurate is it? Repeating the argument of @exr-int-midpoint along each axis gives one error term per axis,
$$
I - M_N \approx \frac{h^2}{24}\sum_{k=1}^{d}\int_{[0,1]^d}\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_k^2}(x)\,dx.
$$
Since $h = 1/m = N^{-1/d}$, the error falls like $N^{-2/d}$.

::: {#exr-int-curse}
## The curse of dimensionality
The product midpoint rule on the cube $[0, 1]^d$ uses $m$ points along each axis, $N = m^d$ in all.

a. In dimension $d$, how many times more points does one more correct decimal place cost? Evaluate your answer for $d = 1$, $2$, $10$ and $20$.
b. The integral of the opening paragraph has $d = 20$. How many points does the grid with $m = 10$ have? At $10^9$ evaluations of $f$ a second, how long does the sum take?
c. Halving the cell width divides the error by 4. By what factor does it multiply the running time in (b)?
d. The coarsest grid that can see any variation along an axis has $m = 2$. How many points does it have for $d = 100$?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="The curse of dimensionality"}
A grid rule whose error is $m^{-r}$ per axis has error $N^{-r/d}$ in terms of the total number of points $N = m^d$. The rate gets worse as the dimension grows: one more correct decimal place costs $10^{d/r}$ times as many points.
:::

@fig-int-grid shows the curse of dimensionality for the integral we started with, $e^{-\|x\|^2}$ over $[0, 1]^d$: on the log-log plot the errors fall along lines of slope $-2/d$, which get flatter and flatter as $d$ grows.


```{ojs}
//| output: false
// The product midpoint rule on exp(-|x|^2) in four dimensions, for every m
// with m^d <= 10^6. The integrand is a product, so the grid sum costs nothing.
intGridSeries = {
  const dims = [1, 2, 4, 8]
  const tokens = ["fn", "warn", "alt", "ink"]
  const series = []
  for (let k = 0; k < dims.length; k++) {
    series.push({label: `d = ${dims[k]}`, token: tokens[k], points: gaussianCubeGridErrors(dims[k], 1e6), kind: "scatter"})
  }
  return series
}
```

## Hit or miss {#sec-int-hitmiss}

Can random points do better? We have already seen one method that does not use a grid. In the last chapter, the circle estimator threw random points into a square and counted how many landed in the disk, using the fact that the area of the disk is the area of the square times the probability of landing in it. But an integral is an area too, namely the area under a graph, so the same idea should work here. Suppose $0 \le f \le c$ on $[a, b]$. We draw a point $(X, Y)$ uniformly from the box $[a, b] \times [0, c]$ and record the *hit*
$$
H = \mathbf{1}_{\{Y \le f(X)\}},
$$
which is 1 when the point lands under the curve, and 0 otherwise.

::: {#def-int-hitmiss}
## The hit-or-miss estimator
Given $N$ independent uniform points $(X_i, Y_i)$ in the box $[a, b] \times [0, c]$, with hits $H_i$, estimate $I$ by
$$\hat I_N^{\,\text{HM}} = c\,(b-a)\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} H_i = \text{box area} \times \text{fraction of points under the curve}.$$
:::

The app below draws $N$ points in the box and colors them according to whether they land under the curve.


```{ojs}

  const data = []
  if (hitShow.has("Box")) {
    data.push({x: [g.a, g.b, g.b, g.a, g.a], y: [0, 0, hitC, hitC, 0], type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: "Box", showlegend: false,
      line: {color: chartColors.muted, width: 1.5}, hoverinfo: "skip"})
  }
  if (hitShow.has("Under the curve")) {
    data.push({x: underX, y: underY, type: "scattergl", mode: "markers", name: "Under the curve", showlegend: false,
      marker: {color: chartColors.fn, size: 4}, hoverinfo: "skip"})
  }
  if (hitShow.has("Above the curve")) {
    data.push({x: aboveX, y: aboveY, type: "scattergl", mode: "markers", name: "Above the curve", showlegend: false,
      marker: {color: chartColors.warn, size: 4}, hoverinfo: "skip"})
  }
  if (hitShow.has("f(x)")) {
    data.push({x: curveX, y: curveY, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: "f(x)", showlegend: false,
      line: {color: chartColors.ink, width: 2.5}, hoverinfo: "skip"})
  }

  // The axis follows the box, so a taller box shrinks the curve inside it.
  const pad = 0.03 * (g.b - g.a)
  return hitPlot(data, {
    xaxis: {range: [g.a - pad, g.b + pad], zeroline: false, title: "x"},
    yaxis: {range: [-0.04 * hitC, 1.08 * hitC], zeroline: false},
    hovermode: false,
    // A new integrand or box height resets any zoom; a new sample keeps it.
    uirevision: hitKey + ":" + hitC,
    autosize: true
  })
}
```

Since this is the circle estimator with a box in place of the square, we can analyze it in exactly the same way.

::: {#exr-int-hit}
## Bias and standard error
Suppose $0 \le f \le c$ on $[a, b]$, and let $I = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$. Let $(X_1, Y_1), \ldots, (X_N, Y_N)$ be independent uniform points in the box $[a, b] \times [0, c]$. Let $H_i = 1$ if $Y_i \le f(X_i)$ and $H_i = 0$ otherwise, and let $\hat I_N^{\,\text{HM}} = c\,(b-a)\cdot\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N H_i$ be the hit-or-miss estimator (@def-int-hitmiss).

a. Find $P(H_i = 1)$ and show that $\hat I_N^{\,\text{HM}}$ is unbiased.
b. Find $\text{SE}\big(\hat I_N^{\,\text{HM}}\big)$ in terms of $a, b, c, I$. Where do you use independence?
c. Take $f(x) = \sin x$ on $[0, \pi]$ with $c = 1$, so $I = 2$. Compute the standard error, and the smallest $N$ for which it is at most $0.001$. Compare with @exr-int-sine (b).
d. Take $f(x) = 4\sqrt{1 - x^2}$ on $[0, 1]$ with $c = 4$, so $I = \pi$. Check that you recover the standard error of the circle estimator from the [last chapter](../estimating-pi/#exr-pi-variance).
e. The height $c$ of the box is your choice, as long as $f \le c$. How does choosing a larger $c$ affect $\hat I_N^{\,\text{HM}}$? Which $c$ is best?
f. Check (e) in [the app](#hit-app): for $\sin x$ at $N = 2000$, compare *Standard error* at $c = 1$ and at $c = 4$ with your formula from (b).
:::

You should find that we get the $N^{-1/2}$ rate again, with a constant that gets worse the more of the box lies above the curve. Raising $c$ in the app shows why: a point that lands above the curve tells us nothing about $f$, and a taller box wastes more of its points up there. For $\sin x$ the standard error is about $1.51/\sqrt N$, so three correct decimal places cost about 2.3 million points. The midpoint rule needs only 29! In one dimension, random points are simply a poor choice, just as they were for [computing $\pi$](../estimating-pi/#sec-randomness-slow).

### Hit or miss in many dimensions {#sec-int-ball}

So why bother with random points at all? The reason is that hit-or-miss works in exactly the same way in any dimension. Let $f$ be a function on the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ with $0 \le f \le c$, and let
$$
I = \int_{[0,1]^d} f(x)\,dx.
$$
We draw $X$ uniformly from the cube, which just means drawing each of its $d$ coordinates independently and uniformly, and we draw $Y$ uniformly from $[0, c]$. As before, we record a hit $H = 1$ when $Y \le f(X)$, and we estimate $I$ by $c$ times the fraction of hits,
$$
\hat I_N^{\,\text{HM}} = \frac{c}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} H_i.
$$

::: {#exr-int-hit-dimension}
## The rate does not see the dimension
a. Show that $\hat I_N^{\,\text{HM}}$ is unbiased with standard error $\sqrt{I\,(c - I)/N}$. Where does the dimension $d$ appear in your argument?
b. Compare with the $N^{-2/d}$ rate of the [product midpoint rule](#sec-int-curse). For which dimensions $d$ does hit-or-miss have the better rate? 
:::

You should find that the dimension does not appear anywhere in the argument. The rate is $N^{-1/2}$ in *every dimension*, and it beats the midpoint rule's $N^{-2/d}$ as soon as $d > 4$. This is the reason why random sampling is the standard tool for high-dimensional integrals, even though it is nearly useless for one-dimensional ones.

Have we escaped the curse of dimensionality, then? Not quite. The rate does not depend on the dimension, but the constant in front of it does, and it can be enormous. A good example is the volume $V_d$ of the unit ball in $d$ dimensions. We can estimate it just as we estimated the area of the disk: draw uniform points in the cube $[-1, 1]^d$, which has volume $2^d$, call a point a *hit* if it lands in the ball, and multiply the fraction of hits by $2^d$. To keep the formulas simple, let us only look at even dimensions $d = 2k$. The exact value is then known to be $V_{2k} = \pi^k/k!$, so we can check our estimates.

::: {#exr-int-ball}
## The ball in the cube
Let $V_d$ be the volume of the unit ball in $d$ dimensions, and let $p_d = V_d/2^d$ be the probability that a uniform point of the cube $[-1, 1]^d$ lands in the ball. The *relative standard error* of an estimator is its standard error divided by the quantity it estimates.

a. Compute $p_d$ for $d = 2$, $d = 10$ and $d = 20$. How does it behave as $d$ grows?
b. Find the relative standard error of the hit-or-miss estimator of $V_d$ with $N$ points, in terms of $p_d$ and $N$. For each $d$ in (a), find the smallest $N$ for which it is at most $0.1$.
c. Take $d = 20$ and draw $N = 10^5$ points. How many hits do you expect? What does the estimator return when there are none, and what is its *estimated* standard error then?
:::

You should find that the fraction of the cube filled by the ball shrinks faster than exponentially in $d$, and the number of points we need grows just as fast: 27 points at $d = 2$, about 40,000 at $d = 10$, and about $4 \times 10^9$ at $d = 20$. In twenty dimensions, 100,000 points give about $0.0025$ hits on average, so we should expect every one of them to miss the ball. The estimate is then 0, and worse, the estimated standard error is also 0, so the method reports a wrong answer with complete confidence! What is going on is that in high dimensions nearly all of the volume of a cube *sits in its corners*, far from the ball, and so uniform points spend almost all of their time where the integrand vanishes.

So even though  the rate does not depend on the dimension, but the number of points we need still does: it grows like $1/p_d$. One way out is to sample more often where the integrand is large and then correct for this, an idea called *importance sampling*, which we will study in [Variance reduction](../variance-reduction/). Another is to make better use of the samples we already have, and this is what we turn to next.


## The sample-mean estimator {#sec-int-mean}

There is a more direct way to write $I = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ as an expectation. Recall the *law of the unconscious statistician*: if $X$ has density $p$, then
$$\mathbb{E}[f(X)] = \int f(x)\,p(x)\,dx.$$
If $X$ is uniform on $[a, b]$, then $p(x) = 1/(b-a)$ on the interval, and so
$$\mathbb{E}[f(X)] = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \frac{I}{b-a}.$$
In other words, the integral is the width of the interval times the *average height* of $f$. The same is true in any dimension:

::: {.callout-important title="An integral is an expectation"}
If $X$ is uniformly distributed on a region $D$ of volume $|D|$, then
$$\int_D f(x)\,dx = |D|\;\mathbb{E}[f(X)],$$
so an average of $f$ over random points of $D$, times $|D|$, estimates the integral.
:::

This is exactly the kind of statement the Monte Carlo principle asks for. Replacing the expectation by a sample average gives our second estimator, which needs neither a box nor the extra coordinate $Y$.

::: {#def-int-mean}
## The sample-mean estimator
Given $N$ independent uniform points $X_1, \ldots, X_N$ in $[a, b]$, estimate $I = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ by
$$\hat I_N = \frac{b-a}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} f(X_i).$$
:::

Notice that $\hat I_N = \sum_i \frac{b-a}{N}\,f(X_i)$ is the total area of $N$ bars, each of width $(b-a)/N$. So this is a Riemann sum, just like the midpoint rule, except that the heights are measured at random points instead of at the centers of the cells. @fig-int-sample shows it for $\sin x$ on $[0, \pi]$: the points are sorted from left to right, and the $i$-th bar gets the height of the $i$-th point, which is usually not inside its own bar.

```{ojs}
//| output: false
intSamplePoints = 6
intSampleSeed = 1
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// The random points from left to right, with their heights.
intSampleSorted = sortedSample(sampleMeanSample(VM.sampling.seededRandom(intSampleSeed), integrands.sin, intSamplePoints), intSamplePoints)
```

:::: {#fig-int-sample}

```{ojs}
{
  const a = 0
  const b = Math.PI
  const h = (b - a) / intSamplePoints

  const curve = []
  for (let k = 0; k <= 300; k++) {
    const x = a + (b - a) * k / 300
    curve.push({x, y: Math.sin(x)})
  }

  // One bar per point, side by side: bar i has the height of the i-th point
  // from the left, which sits on the curve wherever it was drawn.
  const bars = []
  for (let i = 0; i < intSamplePoints; i++) {
    const left = a + i * h
    bars.push({left, right: left + h, center: left + h / 2, x: intSampleSorted.xs[i], height: intSampleSorted.fs[i]})
  }

  const fill = VM.plotting.alpha(chartColors.fn, 0.15)
  const chart = Plot.plot(VM.plotting.plotOptions({
    width, height: 300, marginLeft: 40, marginBottom: 40,
    x: {domain: [a, b], label: "x", labelAnchor: "center"},
    y: {domain: [0, 1.05], label: null},
    marks: [
      Plot.rect(bars, {x1: "left", x2: "right", y1: 0, y2: "height", fill, stroke: chartColors.fn, strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      Plot.line(curve, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: chartColors.ink, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      // A level line from each point to the middle of its bar's top.
      Plot.link(bars, {x1: "x", x2: "center", y1: "height", y2: "height", stroke: chartColors.alt, strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "3,3"}),
      Plot.dot(bars, {x: "x", y: "height", fill: chartColors.alt, r: 3.5})
    ]
  }))
  return intFigure(chart, [
    {label: "sin x", stroke: chartColors.ink, strokeWidth: 2.5},
    {label: "Bars of width (b − a)/N", marks: [
      {mark: "area", fill},
      {mark: "line", stroke: chartColors.fn, strokeWidth: 1.5}
    ]},
    {label: "Random points Xᵢ", marks: [
      {mark: "line", stroke: chartColors.alt, strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "3,3"},
      {mark: "dot", fill: chartColors.alt, r: 3.5}
    ]}
  ])
}
```

The sample-mean estimator for $\sin x$ on $[0, \pi]$ as a Riemann sum. Each random point gives its height to one bar.

::::

Once again our estimator is an average of i.i.d. samples, so we already know how to analyze it. Let us write
$$
\sigma_f^2 = \text{Var}(f(X)) = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx - \left(\frac{I}{b-a}\right)^2
$$
for the variance of the height of $f$ at a uniform point $X$ of $[a, b]$.

::: {#exr-int-variance}
## Bias and standard error
Let $X_1, \ldots, X_N$ be independent uniform points in $[a, b]$, and let $\hat I_N = \frac{b-a}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(X_i)$ be the sample-mean estimator of $I = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ (@def-int-mean). Write $\sigma_f^2 = \text{Var}(f(X_i))$.

a. Show that $\hat I_N$ is unbiased.
b. Compute $\text{Var}(\hat I_N)$ and $\text{SE}(\hat I_N)$ in terms of $\sigma_f$. Where do you use independence?
c. Take $f(x) = \sin x$ on $[0, \pi]$, so $I = 2$. Compute $\sigma_f^2$ and $\text{SE}(\hat I_N)$.
d. Find the smallest $N$ for which $\text{SE}(\hat I_N) \le 0.001$ in (c).
:::

You should find
$$
\text{SE}(\hat I_N) = \frac{(b-a)\,\sigma_f}{\sqrt N},
$$
which is the $N^{-1/2}$ rate once more. Notice that the constant depends on $f$ only through $\sigma_f$. For $\sin x$ the standard error is about $0.967/\sqrt N$, so three correct decimal places cost about a million points.

There is one new difficulty. For hit-or-miss the samples were Bernoulli, so once we had estimated their mean we also knew their variance. Here $\sigma_f$ is a second unknown integral. In practice we estimate it from the same samples, using their sample standard deviation
$$
s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N \big(f(X_i) - \bar f\,\big)^2}, \qquad \bar f = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N f(X_i),
$$
and we report $(b-a)\,s/\sqrt N$ as the standard error.

::: {#exr-int-clt}
## Confidence intervals
a. Write an approximate 95% confidence interval for $I = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ centered at the sample-mean estimator $\hat I_N$, for large $N$, that uses only the samples $f(X_1), \ldots, f(X_N)$.
b. Use @exr-int-variance (c) to predict the standard error for $\sin x$ at $N = 100$.
:::

### Hit or miss against the sample mean {#sec-int-compare}

We now have two unbiased estimators of the same integral, and they even use the same points $X_i$. Is there any reason to choose one over the other? Both have the $N^{-1/2}$ rate, so any difference must be in the constants. Let us first compare them on an example, and then ask whether what we see there is an accident.

::: {#exr-int-hitmiss}
## Hit or miss against the sample mean
Let $I = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ with $0 \le f \le c$. With $N$ points each, let $\hat I_N^{\,\text{HM}}$ be the hit-or-miss estimator of $I$ with box height $c$ (@def-int-hitmiss), and $\hat I_N$ the sample-mean estimator (@def-int-mean).

a. Take $f(x) = \sin x$ on $[0, \pi]$ with $c = 1$. Use @exr-int-hit (c) and @exr-int-variance (c) to compute the standard error of each estimator at $N = 100$. Which is smaller? How many times more points does the other one need to match it?
b. Is (a) special to $\sin x$? Use @exr-int-hit (b) and @exr-int-variance (b) to write $\text{Var}(\hat I_N^{\,\text{HM}}) - \text{Var}(\hat I_N)$ as a single integral over $[a, b]$, for a general $f$ with $0 \le f \le c$. Can you tell its sign? For which functions $f$ is it zero?
c. Take $f(x) = 4\sqrt{1 - x^2}$ on $[0, 1]$ with $c = 4$, so that $I = \pi$ and hit-or-miss is the circle estimator. Compute both variances. How many times more points does hit-or-miss need for the same standard error?
:::

You should find that $\text{Var}(\hat I_N)$ is never larger than $\text{Var}(\hat I_N^{\,\text{HM}})$. The algebra in (b) proves this, but it does not really explain it. The explanation is in how hit-or-miss uses a point $(X, Y)$: all it asks is whether $Y \le f(X)$. Given $X$, the hit $H$ is a coin flip with success probability $f(X)/c$. So $c\,H$ is a noisy stand-in for the height $f(X)$: it is right on average, but it is only ever $0$ or $c$. Hit-or-miss therefore has two sources of randomness, the choice of $X$ and the coin flip, whereas the sample mean has only the first, because it uses $f(X)$ itself. The extra variance of hit-or-miss is the variance of the coin flip! The next exercise turns this observation into a proof.

::: {#exr-int-conditioning}
## Why the sample mean wins
Let $(X, Y)$ be a single uniform point in the box $[a, b] \times [0, c]$, and let $H$ be its hit: $H = 1$ if $Y \le f(X)$ and $H = 0$ otherwise. Write
$$
Z^{\text{HM}} = c\,(b-a)\,H \qquad\text{and}\qquad Z = (b-a)\,f(X)
$$
for what this one point contributes to each estimator, so that $\hat I_N^{\,\text{HM}}$ is the average of $N$ independent copies of $Z^{\text{HM}}$, and $\hat I_N$ is the average of $N$ independent copies of $Z$.

a. Show that $\mathbb{E}[Z^{\text{HM}} \mid X] = Z$.
b. Use the [law of total variance](../probability-review/#sec-conditioning), conditioning on $X$, to show $\text{Var}(Z^{\text{HM}}) \ge \text{Var}(Z)$, without computing an integral.
c. Compute $\mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(Z^{\text{HM}} \mid X)]$ and check that it is $N$ times the difference you found in @exr-int-hitmiss (b).
d. In (b) you never used the form of $H$. State the general fact you proved.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Conditioning reduces variance"}
If we replace a random variable by its conditional expectation, the mean stays the same and the variance goes down. 
:::

In statistics this trick is known as *Rao-Blackwellization*. In our case we conditioned on $X$: the sample mean is just hit-or-miss with each hit $H_i$ replaced by its conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}[H_i \mid X_i] = f(X_i)/c$. @fig-int-hitmiss runs both estimators on the quarter circle. Both errors fall along lines of slope $-1/2$, and the two lines stay a fixed distance apart on the log scale. That distance is the ratio of standard errors you found in @exr-int-hitmiss (c).


```{ojs}
//| output: false
intHitErrors = integrandErrors(VM.sampling.seededRandom(21), integrands.circle, intCounts, 200)
intHitSeries = [
  {label: "Hit or miss", token: "warn", points: intHitErrors.hitMiss, kind: "band"},
  {label: "Sample mean", token: "fn", points: intHitErrors.sampleMean, kind: "band"}
]
```

:::: {#fig-int-hitmiss}

<div class="ojs-chart-block ojs-svg-block">

```{ojs}
  xDomain: [10, 10000], yDomain: [0.001, 10], xLabel: "Points (N)", yLabel: "|estimate − π|"})
```

```{ojs}
  const stats = intOrderStats(intHitSeries)
  stats.push({label: "Error ratio", value: (intHitErrors.hitMiss[last].error / intHitErrors.sampleMean[last].error).toFixed(2),
    title: "RMS error of hit-or-miss divided by RMS error of the sample mean, at N = 10,000"})

}
```

</div>

Two estimators of $\pi = \int_0^1 4\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx$: the RMS error over 200 runs, and the band holding the middle 80% of runs.

::::


## What makes an integrand hard? {#sec-int-hard}

The standard error $(b-a)\,\sigma_f/\sqrt N$ tells us that Monte Carlo sees the integrand only through its variance. What kind of functions have a large variance? In numerical analysis we learn that smooth functions are easy to integrate and rapidly oscillating ones are hard. Is the same true here?

::: {#exr-int-blind}
## Monte Carlo is blind to smoothness
Let $k$ be a positive integer and $f(x) = \sin^2(kx)$ on $[0, \pi]$. Compute the standard error of the sample-mean estimator $\hat I_N$ of $\int_0^\pi f(x)\,dx$ algebraically, by evaluating the integrals for $\sigma_f^2 = \text{Var}(f(X))$, where $X$ is uniform on $[0, \pi]$.
:::

You should find that the standard error is independent of the frequency $k$. This may come as a surprise, but it makes sense once we notice that the variance $\sigma_f^2$ depends only on the distribution of the *values* of $f$, and not on the order in which these values occur along the axis. We could cut the graph into pieces and shuffle them around, and Monte Carlo would not notice.

::: {#exr-int-blind-distribution}
## Same values, different order
Let $X$ be uniform on $[0, \pi]$. Explain why $\sin^2(kX)$ has the same distribution for every nonzero integer $k$.
:::

Oscillation can still hurt Monte Carlo, but for a different reason.

::: {#exr-int-oscillation}
## Cancellation
Let $f_k(x) = k \sin(kx)$ on $[0, \pi]$, with $k$ an odd positive integer. Let $\hat I_N$ be the sample-mean estimator of its integral with $N$ points, and $\sigma_{f_k}^2 = \text{Var}(f_k(X))$ for $X$ uniform on $[0, \pi]$.

a. Compute $I = \int_0^\pi f_k(x)\,dx$.
b. Compute $\sigma_{f_k}^2$ and $\text{SE}(\hat I_N)$. How does the standard error grow with $k$?
c. By what factor is the standard error at $k = 25$ larger than at $k = 1$?
d. How many points does $k = 25$ need for $\text{SE}(\hat I_N) \le 0.01$?
e. The positive and negative lobes of $f_k$ nearly cancel. Explain why cancellation is expensive for an average of random samples.
:::

You should find that the standard error grows like $k$. The integral stays at 2 for every $k$, but the values we are averaging swing between $-k$ and $k$, and we are relying on them to cancel. @fig-int-oscillation shows the two cases $k = 1$ and $k = 25$. The slopes are the same, as they must be, and the constants differ by the factor of about 57 from part (c).

::: {.callout-important title="The variance decides"}
For Monte Carlo, an integrand is hard when its values are spread far from their mean, compared with the size of the integral. Whether it is smooth or not plays no role.
:::


```{ojs}
//| output: false
// f_k(x) = k sin(kx) on [0, pi], integral 2 for odd k. Only the sample-mean
// errors are used; `max` serves the unused hit-or-miss half.
intOscErrors = {
  const out = []
  for (const k of [1, 25]) {
    const integrand = {f: x => k * Math.sin(k * x), a: 0, b: Math.PI, max: k, exact: 2}
    out.push(integrandErrors(VM.sampling.seededRandom(22), integrand, intCounts, 200).sampleMean)
  }
  return out
}
intOscSeries = [
  {label: "25 sin(25x)", token: "alt", points: intOscErrors[1], kind: "band"},
  {label: "sin x", token: "fn", points: intOscErrors[0], kind: "band"}
]
```

:::: {#fig-int-oscillation}

<div class="ojs-chart-block ojs-svg-block">

```{ojs}

  xDomain: [10, 10000], yDomain: [0.001, 100], xLabel: "Points (N)", yLabel: "|estimate − 2|"})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const last = intCounts.length - 1
  const stats = intOrderStats(intOscSeries)
  stats.push({label: "Error ratio", value: (intOscErrors[1][last].error / intOscErrors[0][last].error).toFixed(1),
    title: "RMS error for 25 sin(25x) divided by RMS error for sin x, at N = 10,000"})
  return VM.ui.statRow(stats)
}
```

</div>

The sample-mean estimator on $\int_0^\pi k\sin(kx)\,dx = 2$ for $k = 1$ and $k = 25$: RMS error over 200 runs, with the middle 80% of runs.

::::

Since we do not know $\sigma_f$ in advance, it is useful to have a bound on it that does not require computing an integral.

::: {#exr-int-popoviciu}
## A bound on the variance
Suppose $m \le f(x) \le M$ on $[a, b]$. Let $X$ be uniform on $[a, b]$ and write $Z = f(X)$, so that $\sigma_f^2 = \text{Var}(Z)$.

a. Show that $\text{Var}(Z) \le \mathbb{E}[(Z - c)^2]$ for every constant $c$.
b. Choose $c$ to conclude that $\sigma_f^2 \le (M - m)^2/4$.
c. Which random variables $Z$ with values in $[m, M]$ attain the bound? Relate your answer to hit-or-miss.
d. Let $\hat I_N$ be the sample-mean estimator of $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ with $N$ points. Give a sample size $N$, in terms of $a$, $b$, $m$, $M$ and $\varepsilon$, that guarantees $\text{SE}(\hat I_N) \le \varepsilon$ for every such $f$.
e. For $\sin x$ on $[0, \pi]$, by what factor does (d) overestimate the $N$ actually needed?
:::

You should find that the worst case is a variable that only takes the two extreme values $m$ and $M$, each with probability $1/2$: a fair coin! So among all integrands with a given range, the indicator functions that hit-or-miss uses are the hardest ones.

Let us now return to the midpoint rule of [the first section](#sec-int-grid). It earns its $N^{-2}$ rate from the smoothness of $f$; recall that the derivation in @exr-int-midpoint needed $f''$. This is the exact opposite of what we saw in @exr-int-blind: a grid exploits smoothness, while random points ignore it.

::: {#exr-int-grid-random}
## Random against evenly spaced points
Take $\sin x$ on $[0, \pi]$.

a. How many random points does the sample-mean estimator need for its standard error (@exr-int-variance) to match the error of the midpoint rule at $N = 100$ (@exr-int-sine (a))?
b. Solve for the $N$ at which the standard error equals the midpoint rule's error. Is there any $N$ at which random points win?
:::

You should find that 100 evenly spaced points are worth more than $10^8$ random ones, and that the two errors cross below $N = 1$. In other words, for a smooth integrand in one dimension, random points never win. @fig-int-midpoint shows the two side by side.

```{ojs}
  {label: "Sample mean (random points)", token: "fn", points: intOscErrors[0], kind: "band"},
  {label: "Midpoint rule", token: "warn", points: midpointErrors(Math.sin, 0, Math.PI, 2, intCounts), kind: "scatter"}
]
```

## Many dimensions {#sec-int-dimension}

Just like hit-or-miss, the sample mean works in any dimension. Let $f$ again be a function on the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$, with $I = \int_{[0,1]^d} f(x)\,dx$. Since the cube has volume 1, we simply have $I = \mathbb{E}[f(U)]$ for $U$ uniform on the cube.

::: {#def-int-cube}
## The sample-mean estimator on the cube
Given $N$ independent uniform points $U_1, \ldots, U_N$ in $[0, 1]^d$, estimate $I$ by
$$\hat I_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} f(U_i).$$
:::

Notice that the argument of @exr-int-variance never used the dimension either. So $\hat I_N$ is unbiased with $\text{SE}(\hat I_N) = \sigma_f/\sqrt N$, where $\sigma_f^2 = \text{Var}(f(U))$, and the rate is $N^{-1/2}$ in every dimension. Whatever effect the dimension has must therefore be hiding in the constant $\sigma_f$. For [the ball](#sec-int-ball) we saw this constant explode. Fortunately, for smooth integrands it grows far more slowly.

### The constant depends on the dimension {#sec-int-constant}

The integral we started the chapter with is a good example, because for it we can compute exactly how the constant grows. The integrand is a product,
$$
f(x) = e^{-\|x\|^2} = \prod_{k=1}^d g(x_k), \qquad g(t) = e^{-t^2},
$$
and the two numbers we need are
$$
\alpha = \int_0^1 g(t)\,dt \approx 0.7468, \qquad \beta = \int_0^1 g(t)^2\,dt \approx 0.5981.
$$

::: {#exr-int-product}
## A product integrand
Let $f(x) = \prod_{k=1}^d g(x_k)$ on the cube $[0, 1]^d$, with $\alpha = \int_0^1 g(t)\,dt$ and $\beta = \int_0^1 g(t)^2\,dt$ as above. Let $U$ be uniform on the cube, $I = \int_{[0,1]^d} f(x)\,dx$, and $\hat I_N$ the sample-mean estimator of $I$ with $N$ points (@def-int-cube).

a. Show that $I = \alpha^d$ and $\mathbb{E}[f(U)^2] = \beta^d$. Where do you use independence?
b. The *relative* standard error is $\text{SE}(\hat I_N)/I$. Show that it equals $\sqrt{(\rho^d - 1)/N}$ with $\rho = \beta/\alpha^2$.
c. Show that $\rho \ge 1$ for every function $g$. When is $\rho = 1$?
d. For $g(t) = e^{-t^2}$, $\rho \approx 1.0724$. How many points give a relative standard error of 1% for $d = 1$, $d = 10$, $d = 20$ and $d = 100$?
e. The product midpoint rule reaches 1% relative error at $d = 10$ with $m = 7$ points per axis. How many points is that?
:::

You should find that the number of points needed for a fixed relative accuracy grows like $\rho^d$. This is exponential in the dimension, just like the grid's $m^d$, but with a base that is barely above 1. At $d = 10$, Monte Carlo needs about $10^4$ points where the grid needs $7^{10} \approx 2.8 \times 10^8$. You will often hear that Monte Carlo is immune to the curse of dimensionality. We now see that this is true of the rate but not of the constant, and how fast the constant grows depends on the integrand: like $\rho^d$ here, and like $1/p_d$ for the ball.

@fig-int-dimension compares random points with the product midpoint rule on this integral. Move the slider to change $d$ and watch the grid fall behind.

## Watching the curse
a. In @fig-int-dimension, does the fitted order of the grid match the $N^{-2/d}$ rate of the [product midpoint rule](#sec-int-curse) as you change $d$?
b. At $N = 10^4$, find the smallest $d$ for which random points beat the grid. Is it the dimension of @exr-int-hit-dimension (b)? Why might it differ?

The principle of integrating out what we can (@exr-int-conditioning) also explains a trick from the last chapter.

::: {#exr-int-gauss}
## Gauss's circle, revisited
The [Gauss circle method](../estimating-pi/#sec-gauss-circle) estimates $\pi$ by $L(r)/r^2$, where $L(r)$ counts the integer points in the disk of radius $r$. Its observed error is about $r^{-3/2}$.

a. Counted point by point, the method tests $N = (2r+1)^2$ grid points. Write its error as a power of $N$.
b. The [one-loop count](../estimating-pi/#exr-gauss-count) of the last chapter sums $2\lfloor\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}\rfloor + 1$ over $2r + 1$ values of $x$. Write its error as a power of the number of loop steps.
c. Show that the one-loop count is, up to rounding, a Riemann sum for the one-dimensional integral $\int_{-1}^{1} 2\sqrt{1 - t^2}\,dt = \pi$.
d. Which estimator of @exr-int-hitmiss does each count correspond to? What was integrated out?
:::


## Quasi-random points {#sec-int-qmc}

We now have two kinds of points, each with its own strength. Grid points are spread evenly, and this evenness is what gives the midpoint rule its fast rate. But a grid has to be built all at once, with $m^d$ points, and its rate gets worse as $d$ grows. Random points can be added one at a time in any dimension, but they clump together and leave gaps, and we pay for this with the slow rate $N^{-1/2}$. Can we have the best of both? In the last chapter we met a third kind of points, the [Halton points](../estimating-pi/#sec-halton), which arrive one at a time and still spread evenly. Such points are called *quasi-random*, and using them in place of random points is called *quasi-Monte Carlo* [@niederreiter1992; @caflisch1998]. In this section we make precise what "spread evenly" means, and see what it buys us.

### The van der Corput and Halton sequences {#sec-int-halton}

The construction starts in one dimension, with a surprisingly simple idea: write the integers backwards.

::: {#def-int-vdc}
## The van der Corput sequence
Fix a base $b \ge 2$ and write $n$ in base $b$, $n = a_0 + a_1 b + a_2 b^2 + \cdots$ with digits $0 \le a_k < b$. The *radical inverse* of $n$ mirrors the digits about the radix point:
$$
\varphi_b(n) = \frac{a_0}{b} + \frac{a_1}{b^2} + \frac{a_2}{b^3} + \cdots.
$$
The van der Corput sequence in base $b$ is $\varphi_b(1), \varphi_b(2), \varphi_b(3), \ldots$
:::

For example, $6 = 110_2$ in binary, and reversing the digits gives $\varphi_2(6) = 0.011_2 = 3/8$.

::: {#exr-int-vdc}
## Counting backwards
a. Compute $\varphi_2(n)$ for $n = 1, \ldots, 8$ and mark the points on $[0, 1]$ in order. Describe in words where each new point lands.
b. Show that $\varphi_2(0), \varphi_2(1), \ldots, \varphi_2(2^k - 1)$ are exactly the grid points $j/2^k$, $j = 0, \ldots, 2^k - 1$, in some order.
c. Show more: among any $2^k$ *consecutive* terms of the sequence, each interval $[j/2^k, (j+1)/2^k)$ contains exactly one. Which digits of $n$ decide the interval?
d. To fill the square we need pairs. Why is $(\varphi_2(n), \varphi_2(n))$ useless? Show that the points $(\varphi_2(n), \varphi_3(n))$ put exactly one of any $2^j 3^k$ consecutive points in each box $[\tfrac{p}{2^j}, \tfrac{p+1}{2^j}) \times [\tfrac{q}{3^k}, \tfrac{q+1}{3^k})$. Which theorem about remainders do you need?
:::

Part (c) is the whole point of the construction. The sequence behaves like a grid at every scale at once, and it completes a finer grid each time $n$ passes a power of $b$. Part (d) explains why the bases must have no common factor, and tells us how to go to higher dimensions.

::: {#def-int-halton}
## The Halton sequence
Let $b_1, \ldots, b_d$ be the first $d$ primes. The Halton sequence in $[0, 1)^d$ is
$$
x_n = \big(\varphi_{b_1}(n), \ldots, \varphi_{b_d}(n)\big), \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots
$$
:::

### Discrepancy {#sec-int-discrepancy}

How can we measure whether a set of points is spread evenly? If it is, then every region should receive its fair share of the points: the fraction of points in the region should be close to its volume. We test this on all boxes with a corner at the origin, and record the worst case.

::: {#def-int-discrepancy}
## Star discrepancy
For points $x_1, \ldots, x_N$ in $[0, 1]^d$ and a corner $t = (t_1, \ldots, t_d)$ in the cube, write $B_t = [0, t_1) \times \cdots \times [0, t_d)$. The *local discrepancy* at $t$ is the difference between the fraction of points in the box and its volume, and the *star discrepancy* is its largest size:
$$
D_N^* = \sup_{t \in [0,1]^d}\;\left|\,\frac{\#\{i : x_i \in B_t\}}{N} - t_1 t_2 \cdots t_d\,\right|.
$$
:::

In the app below you can drag the corner of the box. The readouts show the fraction of points in the box, the area of the box, and the difference between the two, which is the local discrepancy. The star discrepancy is the worst local discrepancy over all positions of the corner.

::: {#exr-int-discrepancy}
## Three kinds of points
Recall from @def-int-discrepancy that for points $x_1, \ldots, x_N$ in $[0, 1]^d$, the local discrepancy at a corner $t$ is the fraction of the points in the box $B_t = [0, t_1) \times \cdots \times [0, t_d)$ minus the volume of the box, and the star discrepancy $D_N^*$ is its largest absolute value over all $t$.

a. In one dimension, compute $D_N^*$ for the midpoint grid $x_j = (j - \tfrac12)/N$. For which $t$ is the local discrepancy largest?
b. For $N$ random points in $[0, 1]$ and a fixed $t$, what is the distribution of the number of points in $[0, t)$? Find the standard deviation of the local discrepancy at $t$. How does it scale with $N$?
c. Now in the square, with [the app](#qmc-app) at $N = 100$: record *Star discrepancy* for the random points, the grid, and the Halton points with bases 2 and 3. Repeat at $N = 1000$. Which improves fastest?
d. The $m \times m$ midpoint grid has $N = m^2$ points. Find a box $B_t$ of area $1/(2m)$ that contains none of them, and conclude that $D_N^* \ge 1/(2\sqrt N)$. Find the box in the app. What is the corresponding bound in $d$ dimensions?
:::

You should find that $D_N^* = 1/(2N)$ for the midpoint grid in one dimension (and in fact no set of $N$ points can do better), whereas random points have a local discrepancy of order $N^{-1/2}$. Part (d) is the curse of dimensionality again, this time seen through discrepancy: in $d$ dimensions a grid has $D_N^* \ge 1/(2N^{1/d})$, because the slabs between its layers contain no points at all. So already in the square, a grid is hardly more evenly spread than random points. The Halton points do better than both, and the next theorem tells us by how much.

::: {#thm-int-halton}
## Discrepancy of the Halton sequence
For every dimension $d$ there is a constant $C_d$ such that the first $N$ points of the Halton sequence in $[0, 1)^d$ satisfy
$$
D_N^* \le C_d\,\frac{(\log N)^d}{N} \qquad \text{for all } N \ge 2
$$
[@halton1960; @niederreiter1992].
:::

@fig-int-discrepancy compares the three kinds of points in one dimension, where the Halton sequence is just the van der Corput sequence in base 2.

```{ojs}
  {label: "Midpoint grid", token: "warn", points: intDiscrepancy.grid, kind: "scatter"}
]
```

::: {#rem-int-ks .remark}
## A statistic you know
You may have met $D_N^*$ before. In one dimension it is the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic for testing whether $x_1, \ldots, x_N$ are a sample from the uniform distribution, namely the largest gap between their empirical distribution function and $t$. For truly random points, $\sqrt N\,D_N^*$ converges in distribution to a limit with mean about $0.87$. Quasi-random points fail this test, but in an unusual direction: they are far too uniform to be random!
:::

### Even points integrate well {#sec-int-koksma}

Why should a small discrepancy lead to a small integration error? In one dimension the two are related by an exact identity, and all it takes to prove it is one integration by parts.

::: {#exr-int-koksma}
## Koksma's inequality
Let $f$ be continuously differentiable on $[0, 1]$, let $x_1, \ldots, x_N$ be any points in $[0, 1]$, and let $F_N(t)$ be the fraction of the points that are less than $t$.

a. Show that $f(x_i) = f(1) - \int_0^1 \mathbf{1}_{\{x_i < t\}}\,f'(t)\,dt$.
b. Average (a) over $i$ to express $\frac1N\sum_i f(x_i)$ through $F_N$.
c. Integrate by parts to show that $\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx = f(1) - \int_0^1 t\,f'(t)\,dt$.
d. Subtract, and conclude that
$$
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} f(x_i) - \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx = -\int_0^1 \big(F_N(t) - t\big)\,f'(t)\,dt.
$$
e. Deduce that
$$
\left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} f(x_i) - \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx\right| \le D_N^*\int_0^1 |f'(t)|\,dt,
$$
where $D_N^*$ is the star discrepancy of the points (@def-int-discrepancy).
f. The integral $V(f) = \int_0^1 |f'(t)|\,dt$ is the *total variation* of $f$. Describe it in words for a function that rises from 0 to 1 and falls back to 0, $k$ times. Compute $V(f)$ for $f(u) = \sin^2(k\pi u)$.
:::

The identity in (d) is quite remarkable: it writes the integration error as the local discrepancy of the points, weighted by the slope of $f$. The bound in (e) continues to hold in every dimension, once we find the right notion of variation.

::: {#thm-int-koksma}
## The Koksma-Hlawka inequality
Let $f$ have bounded variation $V(f)$ on $[0, 1]^d$ in the sense of Hardy and Krause. Then for any points $x_1, \ldots, x_N$ in $[0, 1]^d$,
$$
\left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} f(x_i) - \int_{[0,1]^d} f(x)\,dx\right| \le V(f)\,D_N^*
$$
[@niederreiter1992].
:::

Here the variation in the sense of Hardy and Krause is the $d$-dimensional analogue of $\int |f'|$, and is built from the mixed partial derivatives of $f$. All we need to know about it is that it is finite for smooth functions.

::: {.callout-important title="Error ≤ variation × discrepancy"}
The Koksma-Hlawka inequality splits the error into two factors: one depends only on the integrand, and the other only on the points. With Halton points the error is $O\big((\log N)^d/N\big)$, which is almost $N^{-1}$, compared with $N^{-1/2}$ for random points.
:::

It is worth comparing this with the Monte Carlo error $\sigma_f/\sqrt N$. In both cases the error is a property of $f$ times a property of the points, but the two methods care about different properties of $f$.

::: {#exr-int-qmc-mc}
## Variation against variance
Take $f(u) = \sin^2(k\pi u)$ on $[0, 1]$, the integrand of @exr-int-blind rescaled to the unit interval. Recall that $\sigma_f^2 = \text{Var}(f(U))$ for $U$ uniform on $[0, 1]$, and that $V(f) = \int_0^1 |f'(t)|\,dt$ is the total variation of $f$.

a. How do $\sigma_f$ and $V(f)$ depend on $k$?
b. Which method's error bound feels the frequency $k$? Is that consistent with @exr-int-midpoint?
c. A bound, unlike a standard error, is a guarantee. What does the Koksma-Hlawka inequality guarantee that a 95% confidence interval does not? What does it cost to evaluate?
:::

::: {#rem-int-indicator .remark}
## Why the circle was slower
The indicator function of a disk jumps along a curve, and it turns out that its variation in the sense of Hardy and Krause is infinite, so @thm-int-koksma tells us nothing about it. This is why the Halton points in the last chapter estimated $\pi$ at a rate of only about $N^{-3/4}$ rather than $N^{-1}$. So hit-or-miss integrands are the worst case for quasi-Monte Carlo, just as they were for Monte Carlo (@exr-int-popoviciu). Integrating out a variable (@exr-int-conditioning) leaves us with a smoother integrand, and this helps quasi-random points even more than it helps random ones.
:::

### Does it survive the dimension? {#sec-int-qmc-dimension}

You may have noticed that in the bound $(\log N)^d/N$ the dimension is back in an exponent. Should we be worried?

::: {#exr-int-qmc-dimension}
## The fine print
Let $g(N) = (\ln N)^d/N$, the bound of @thm-int-halton for $N$ Halton points in dimension $d$, without its constant.

a. Show that $g$ *increases* until $N = e^d$. Evaluate $e^d$ for $d = 10$ and $d = 30$.
b. For $d = 10$, show that $g(N) < N^{-1/2}$ requires $\ln N > 20 \ln \ln N$, and solve this numerically. Is such an $N$ feasible?
c. Does (b) show that Halton points are worse than random points in ten dimensions for feasible $N$? What exactly does it show?
:::

You should find that for $d = 10$ the bound does not fall below the Monte Carlo rate until about $N = 10^{39}$, which is hopeless. But a bound that tells us nothing is not the same as a method that fails. Let us see what actually happens: @fig-int-qmc runs the Halton points on the Gaussian integral of @fig-int-dimension.

<div class="ojs-panel ojs-grid">

```{ojs}
viewof qmcDim = {

  return slider
}
```

::::

::: {#exr-int-qmc-figure}
## Halton points in practice
a. In @fig-int-qmc, how does the fitted order of the Halton points change as $d$ goes from 1 to 10? Compare it with the grid's.
b. At $d = 10$ and $N = 10^5$, by what factor do the Halton points beat the Monte Carlo standard error? How many random points would match them?
c. In [the app](#qmc-app), choose *Halton, bases 17 and 19* at $N = 100$. What do you see? Explain it from @def-int-vdc: what are $\varphi_{17}(n)$ and $\varphi_{19}(n)$ for $n < 17$? Compare *Star discrepancy* with the random points.
d. In which coordinates of a high-dimensional Halton sequence does the problem of (c) appear, and until which $N$?
:::

You should find that on this smooth integrand the Halton points keep an order near $0.9$ all the way through ten dimensions, which is far better than @thm-int-halton promises for these values of $N$. Their weakness shows up in part (c): a pair of large prime bases starts out on a few parallel lines, and it takes roughly the product of the two bases in points before the square is filled. Modern quasi-random sequences, such as Sobol' points and scrambled Halton points, are designed to avoid this problem. It is also the reason why quasi-Monte Carlo has to be used with care beyond a few dozen dimensions.

### Putting the randomness back {#sec-int-rqmc}

Quasi-Monte Carlo gives us a better estimate, but no way of knowing how good it is. There is no standard error, because nothing is random, and the bound $V(f)\,D_N^*$ is harder to compute than the integral itself. Fortunately, a small dose of randomness fixes this without spoiling the evenness of the points [@cranley1976].

::: {#def-int-shift}
## Random shift
Let $x_1, \ldots, x_N$ be quasi-random points in $[0, 1)^d$ and let $U$ be a single uniform point of $[0, 1)^d$. The *shifted* points are $x_i + U \bmod 1$, each coordinate taken modulo 1, and the shifted estimator is
$$
\hat I_N^{\,\text{shift}} = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N f\big(x_i + U \bmod 1\big).
$$
:::

::: {#exr-int-shift}
## Randomized quasi-Monte Carlo
a. Show that for a fixed $x \in [0, 1)$ and $U$ uniform on $[0, 1)$, the number $x + U \bmod 1$ is uniform on $[0, 1)$. Conclude that $\hat I_N^{\,\text{shift}}$ is unbiased.
b. Are the shifted points independent of each other? Does unbiasedness need them to be? Does the formula $\sigma_f/\sqrt N$ for the standard error?
c. A shift moves all the points together. What does it do to the gaps between them, and why should the error stay small?
d. One shifted estimate is one random number, with no standard error of its own. Describe how to get an unbiased estimate of $I$ *and* a standard error for it from $R$ independent shifts. How many function evaluations does it use?
e. Find the randomly shifted Halton points in @fig-int-qmc. Is their fitted order closer to the Halton points' or to Monte Carlo's?
:::

You should find that $R$ independent shifts give $R$ i.i.d. unbiased estimates. Their average and their sample standard deviation then give an estimate and a standard error, exactly as in @exr-int-clt. Notice that the points within a single shift are as far from independent as they could be, and it is precisely this dependence that makes the error small.


## Summary

- In [Grids and the curse of dimensionality](#sec-int-grid) we derived the midpoint rule's $N^{-2}$ error and saw it decay to $N^{-2/d}$ in $d$ dimensions, where one more decimal place costs $10^{d/2}$ times the work.
- In [Hit or miss](#sec-int-hitmiss) we turned the circle estimator into an estimator of any integral. Its rate is $N^{-1/2}$ in every dimension, but its constant [explodes](#sec-int-ball) when the region fills a vanishing fraction of its box.
- In [The sample-mean estimator](#sec-int-mean) we wrote an integral as the interval's width times an average height, found its standard error $(b-a)\,\sigma_f/\sqrt N$, and saw by conditioning that it [always beats hit or miss](#sec-int-compare): integrate out what you can.
- In [What makes an integrand hard?](#sec-int-hard) we saw that Monte Carlo sees only the variance of the values of $f$. It is blind to smoothness and frequency, and what hurts it is cancellation. A grid uses the smoothness that random points ignore, and in one dimension it wins at every $N$.
- In [Many dimensions](#sec-int-dimension) we saw that the sample mean's rate is free of the dimension but [its constant](#sec-int-constant) is not: for a product integrand the work grows like $\rho^d$, slowly enough that random points beat the grid within a few dimensions.
- In [Quasi-random points](#sec-int-qmc) we measured evenness by the star discrepancy, proved in one dimension that the error is at most variation times discrepancy, and saw Halton points reach nearly $N^{-1}$. A [random shift](#sec-int-rqmc) gives them a standard error.

Every method in this chapter assumed a supply of uniform random numbers. The next part, [Sampling](../sampling-overview/), asks where they come from, and how to turn them into samples from other distributions.
